title: Goji berries vs. blueberries: nutrition comparison

seo.title: Goji berries vs. blueberries: nutrition comparison
seo.meta_description: Dried goji and fresh blueberries are unfair to compare ounce-for-ounce without accounting for water. See calories, fiber, sugar and nutrients in realistic portions.
seo.search_intent: Compare dried goji berries and fresh blueberries fairly by nutrition and serving size

excerpt: Dried goji looks far more concentrated per 100 g largely because it contains very little water, while fresh blueberries are about 84% water. In realistic portions, 28 g dried goji provides about 98 calories, 3.6 g fiber and 12.8 g sugar; 150 g fresh blueberries provides about 86 calories, 3.6 g fiber and 14.9 g sugar.
content_html:
Put 100 g of dried goji berries beside 100 g of fresh blueberries and goji appears to dominate almost every nutrient. One detail changes the interpretation: the goji is dried, while blueberries are roughly 84% water.

What 100 g shows

Per 100 gDried gojiFresh blueberries
Calories34957
Protein14.3 g0.7 g
Fiber13.0 g2.4 g
Sugars45.6 g10.0 g
Water7.5 g84.2 g

Drying concentrates everything: fiber and minerals, but also sugar and calories.

A serving comparison tells a different story

Compare 1 oz (28 g) dried goji with 150 g fresh blueberries and the gap shrinks:

ServingGoji 28 gBlueberries 150 g
Calories~98~86
Fiber~3.6 g~3.6 g
Sugars~12.8 g~14.9 g
Protein~4.0 g~1.1 g

The servings now contain almost identical fiber and fairly similar calorie and sugar totals.

Where goji stands out

The USDA dried-goji reference provides 6.8 mg iron and 190 mg calcium per 100 g. A 28 g portion works out to roughly 1.9 mg iron and 53 mg calcium. Protein is also unusually concentrated for a fruit because so much water has been removed.

Where blueberries stand out

Blueberries provide much more food volume for similar calories and contain anthocyanins associated with their blue-purple color. A 150 g serving also provides roughly 15 mg vitamin C.

Which is better?

Dried goji is a compact dried fruit; blueberries are a high-water fresh fruit. Both can fit well in a varied diet.

The more useful lesson is broader: when comparing dried and fresh fruit, account for water before treating the per-100-g table as a serving-size verdict.

Dried and fresh forms are not equivalent comparisons

Goji berries are commonly sold dried, while blueberries are usually eaten fresh or frozen. Removing water concentrates calories, sugar and micronutrients per 100 grams, so a dried-versus-fresh table can exaggerate the impression that one fruit is inherently denser. Comparing normal serving sizes gives a more realistic picture of what people actually eat.

Blueberries bring a different polyphenol profile

The deep blue color comes largely from anthocyanins, a family of plant pigments studied for their antioxidant and signaling effects. Goji berries contain different carotenoids and other polyphenols, including zeaxanthin. These compounds are not interchangeable, which supports dietary variety rather than a winner-takes-all ranking.

Calories matter more with handfuls of dried fruit

Dried goji is easy to snack on quickly because a small volume represents a larger amount of whole fruit. A modest handful can therefore supply substantially more carbohydrate and calories than the same visual volume of fresh blueberries. That is not a problem by itself, but it matters for people tracking energy intake or glucose response.

Frozen blueberries remain nutritionally useful

Freezing makes blueberries available year-round and generally preserves their fiber and many phytochemicals well. They may soften after thawing, but that texture is ideal for oatmeal, yogurt and smoothies. Buying frozen fruit can also be less expensive than out-of-season fresh berries without turning the food into a nutritionally inferior option.

Goji berries can interact with some medications

Case reports and pharmacologic concerns have been raised particularly with warfarin. Anyone taking medication with a narrow therapeutic range should mention frequent use of concentrated herbal or dried-fruit products to a clinician or pharmacist. For most people, small culinary amounts of either berry fit easily into a varied diet.

Neither fruit needs a “superfood” label to be worthwhile

Blueberries are easy to add in a generous fresh or frozen serving, while dried goji works more like a concentrated garnish in oatmeal, yogurt or trail mix. Choosing between them can therefore be based on price, taste, texture and the rest of the meal. A rotating mix of berries and other fruits provides a broader range of pigments and nutrients than repeatedly buying one expensive product for a single headline compound.

Preparation can erase or create differences too. Blueberries in a heavily sweetened muffin are not nutritionally equivalent to plain berries, and goji berries coated in chocolate differ from unsweetened dried fruit. Comparing the fruit itself is useful, but the food built around it may contribute far more sugar, fat or calories than the berry choice ever could.

faq.question: Does goji have more sugar than blueberries?
faq.answer: Per 100 g, yes: about 45.6 g in dried goji versus 10 g in fresh blueberries. In the servings compared here, the totals are about 12.8 g versus 14.9 g.

faq.question: Which has more fiber?
faq.answer: Dried goji wins per 100 g, but a 28 g goji portion and 150 g blueberries both provide about 3.6 g fiber.

faq.question: Does goji have more protein?
faq.answer: Yes. The dried reference contains 14.3 g/100 g, or about 4 g in 28 g, compared with about 1.1 g in 150 g blueberries.

faq.question: Is a 100 g comparison fair?
faq.answer: It is valid for composition by weight but misleading for portions because one food is dehydrated and the other is mostly water.
